newsitem.title: UK: FOCUS-London trades 930 tonnes of gold daily - LBMA.
newsitem.headline: FOCUS-London trades 930 tonnes of gold daily - LBMA.

text.p: Gold bullion deals, transacted worldwide but cleared through London averaged 930 tonnes a day during the final quarter of 1996, according to figures released for the first time by the London Bullion Market Association (LBMA) on Wedndesday.
The release of the data lifted the centuries old veil of secrecy which has surrounded gold dealing and confirmed the London market's supremacy in the business, according to the LBMA.
The value of the gold cleared daily in London was around $10 billion, LBMA chairman Alan Baker said at a presentation to launch the release of the data by the LBMA on a monthly basis.
"We hoped to enhance the transparency of the market without compromising our clients' confidentiality," Baker said.

In May 1994, the Bank of England -- the formal supervisor of the conduct of the London-based bullion market -- carried out a survey of the LBMA's 14 market making members and found they traded on average seven million ounces daily in London.
That compared with three million ounces on New York's Comex futures market and one milion ounces a day on Tokyo's Tocom gold futures market, Baker said.

"It was not practical to do that on a regular basis so the LBMA looked at the numbers settled (in) London here as it is these figures which make London the global clearing centre for gold trading," he said.
"The LBMA sought to measure all forms of (gold) transaction carried out throughout the world and settled in London," Baker said.
The volume of gold cleared through London daily was almost twice the total annual gold mine production of South Africa, the world's leading gold miner, he said.

In another perspective, Baker said its $10-billion a day clearing value was 1/40th the size of the London foreign exchange market, according to the last Bank of England survey conducted in that area in April, 1995.
The LBMA also revealed the silver deals cleared by their eight clearing members in London during the final quarter of last year averaged daily 8,000 tonnes valued at about $1.00 billion.

LBMA chief executive Chris Elston denied that the market had come under pressure from either the Bank of England or its members to lift the cloak of secrecy with which it has traditionally shrouded its dealings.
"There was no pressure. It was a move to mark the trend towards the greater availability of numbers," he said.
Baker said the decision followed the "evolution" of the market and a desire to raise its profile.
"I think it is worthwhile putting this aspect of London trading on the map. The figures demonstrate exactly were we stand," he said.
As well as the monthly clearing figures, the LBMA will release a daily indication of gold lease or borrow rates which measure the availablity or tightness of the market as they rise and fall.
Both the clearance volume data and the lease rate indications will be distributed on Reuters pages, beginning on February 8, 1997.
The LBMA was incorporated in 1987 after the UK's Financial Services Act passed the previous year formalised the Bank of England's supervisory role of the gold market.
